Tenemos experiencia en marketing digital, análisis de datos, gestión de proyectos y herramientas tecnológicas. Nos interesa especialmente explorar cómo la ciencia y la tecnología pueden generar soluciones a desafíos reales.
summary: VYTA is a crew health monitoring station for long-duration Mars missions that runs in the browser of a single laptop, so astronauts can evaluate and act on their own health when Earth is minutes away. It gathers the indicators named in the challenge (blood pressure, heart rate, glucose, temperature, sleep, mood) plus stress, hydration, HRV, respiration, SpO2, reaction time, vestibular stability, visual acuity, cabin radiation dose, CO2/O2 and noise, from manual entry, a simulated smartwatch, the webcam (blink-based fatigue, pulse estimate, skin photo) and cognitive tests. A deterministic rules engine turns them into a green/yellow/orange/red status for nine body zones, compared with each astronaut's personal baseline, and every threshold shows its origin (NASA, NASA-derived, external clinical guideline or team design). VYTA AI, a voice assistant, explains alerts with NASA sources and runs local emergency triage based on ISS medical checklists, without AI or network. A Reports screen prepares the clinical summary for flight surgeons with the 14-minute signal delay. AI can raise an alert but never lower it. Educational prototype, not a medical device.
details:
WHAT IT DOES. VYTA is a crew health monitoring station for a Mars mission (Mars sol = 24 h 37 min). It tells the astronaut what to measure and when, turns every measurement into a deterministic status for nine body zones (heart, lungs, brain, bones and muscle, eyes, immunity and others) using colour plus shape (green circle, yellow triangle, orange diamond, red square) so it is accessible, and explains what to do next. Screens: Overview (general status, active alerts with their NASA source, daily check-in and the VYTA AI voice card), Health (body map with Physical, Mental and Risks views, key indicators, clinical alerts and recommended protocols), Activity (camera-based exercise coach, cognitive exercises and the Jornada), Register (daily check-in, mood, skin photo, visual acuity test for SANS and the 'How do I look today?' facial check), Analytics (trends with reference bands and the astronaut's personal baseline) and Reports (link with Earth).

HOW IT WORKS. (1) A deterministic rules engine (lib/motor) evaluates every reading against thresholds, deviation from the personal baseline and compound rules (for example viral reactivation: average sleep < 6 h + stress >= 7 + a skin symptom). Each rule cites the NASA risk page that explains why it is monitored, and the app shows where each number comes from: NASA, NASA-derived, an external clinical guideline, or team design. (2) VYTA AI is the voice assistant: the astronaut speaks (Gemini transcribes the audio), VYTA AI answers using the day's data and NASA fact sheets with source citations (Claude Haiku 5.5), and the answer is read aloud with the browser's speech synthesis. It can also take a spoken check-in ('log 37 with 6') and fill the measurements. (3) Local emergency triage: red-flag phrases (cardiac arrest, choking, severe allergy, stroke signs, heavy bleeding, self-harm, chest pain, fainting, possible clot) are detected in the browser, with no AI and no network, and VYTA reads the first steps of the ISS medical checklists and alerts the Crew Medical Officer, because an answer from Earth would take about 30 minutes. (4) Camera features run in the browser with MediaPipe: the exercise coach counts repetitions and corrects form with Pose Landmarker, and the facial check measures blinking and PERCLOS (fatigue) and estimates pulse (rPPG) with Face Landmarker; no image leaves the browser without consent. (5) Cognitive exercises: a Go/No-Go reaction test (PVT-style) and a vestibular (VOR) stability test, which feed the cognitive and sensorimotor indicators. (6) Jornada: the mission clock with the 24 h 37 min sol, protected sleep from 22:00 to 06:30, daily and weekly tasks, and notifications by type (routine, alert, Earth) that stay silent at night unless there is a red alert. (7) Reports: the Earth link builds the clinical summary, main findings and a proposed plan from the records and the rules engine, and simulates the 14-minute one-way delay: send, evaluation, and the flight surgeon's reply (simulated in the demo) shown in a message channel. (8) Data: everything is stored offline-first in IndexedDB (Dexie) and synchronized with Supabase (PostgreSQL and Auth). Because there are no real sensors, a simulator generates future sols from documented NASA ranges (HRV, respiration, muscle and bone, cognition, isolation, cabin radiation, CO2/O2) and runs the rules engine as the data arrives; the smartwatch is simulated.

SAFETY BY DESIGN. The AI explains and comments, but the rules engine decides: the engine's level is a mandatory floor, so the AI can raise an alert and never lower it, and the exercise plan has caps per level (orange: light intensity and short sessions; red: rest). VYTA AI does not dose medication. Without internet, or with IA_APAGADA=1, the app keeps working from local rules, local triage, MediaPipe, IndexedDB and a versioned backup of real pre-generated answers, so a demo never depends on the network. This is an educational prototype and not a medical device: thresholds are indicative and configurable, and some clinical cut-offs come from general clinical guidelines because NASA does not publish traffic-light ranges for crew.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT. On a Mars mission, real-time ground support is not available, so the crew carries much of the responsibility for spotting health changes in themselves. VYTA reduces that burden: one place gathers the indicators, shows trends against a personal baseline, explains each alert with traceable NASA sources, tells the astronaut when to self-care, when to alert the Crew Medical Officer and when to escalate to flight surgeons, and keeps working offline. It addresses the four hazards named in the challenge: radiation (cabin dose tracking against the 600 mSv career limit), isolation and confinement (mood, stress, sleep and cognitive tracking), altered gravity (bone, muscle, cardiovascular and vestibular indicators and exercise coaching) and the hostile closed environment (CO2, O2, pressure and noise).

DATA IN THE DEMO. The scenario is 'Sol 42 on Mars' for a fictional astronaut (Ana Ríos), with 60 sols of simulated data. The smartwatch, cabin sensors and radiation dosimeter are simulated and the architecture accepts real sensors. All data is fictional.

TOOLS. Next.js 16 (App Router), React 19, JavaScript, Sass Modules, Recharts; Dexie (IndexedDB) and Supabase (PostgreSQL, Auth, pgvector search over NASA documents); MediaPipe Tasks Vision (Pose and Face Landmarker); Web Speech API speech synthesis; Gemini audio transcription; Anthropic SDK with Claude Haiku 5.5; Node test runner for the clinical logic. Designed for a 1280x800 laptop, the kind of device crews use on the ISS.

CREATIVITY. Every alert is tied to its NASA source and shows the origin of its threshold; an AI-free emergency layer runs locally because of the communication delay; the whole health picture is organized in nine clickable body zones; and the app simulates future sols and the delayed Earth link so the crew experience can be tested end to end.

USE OF SUPER INTELLIGENCE. Claude Haiku 5.5 is part of the product (VYTA AI answers, spoken check-in, facial check and exercise comments) and Gemini transcribes audio; AI answers are identified as AI in the app. The team used Claude Code to help write, review and test code and documentation, and to summarize NASA public pages. No NASA logos or branding were generated or modified. Source code: https://github.com/santi-subidia/nasa-space-buenacom
